newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. wants quick result from PLO-Israel talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wants quick result from PLO-Israel talks.

text.p: The United States urged Israel and the Palestinians to reach concrete results quickly in talks that began on Sunday to salvage U.S.-mediated peace agreements undermined by violence.

U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher, dispatched to the region after an emergency PLO-Israeli summit at the White House last week, said the situation between Israel and the PLO was still dangerous although tensions had eased.
Christopher said Israel's new right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu assured him he would carry out signed agreements with the PLO.
Christopher said he hoped his meeting with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat would help move the peace process forward.
"The recent violence has demonstrated the great urgency of reaching some concrete results just as soon as possible," Christopher told a news conference with Netanyahu in Jerusalem.
After meeting Arafat in the PLO-ruled Gaza Strip Christopher said: "The situation has eased somewhat...but it is still a dangerous situation."
Christopher did not take part in talks between teams of lower-level negotiators that followed at an Israeli-Palestinian liaison office at the Erez crossing between Israel and the Gaza Strip.

Resumption of these talks was the main achievement of President Bill Clinton's hastily convened summit last week to save five years of U.S.-mediated peace talks threatened by violence that killed 58 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers.

Netanyahu, whose opening of a tunnel near Jerusalem's Moslem holy places triggered that violence, said Israel sought a joint recommitment with the Palestinians to their peace accords. But he declined to set a date for a troop redeployment from the West Bank city of Hebron, delayed since March.

"What we seek is a simultaneous recommitment by both sides to the principles that both signed on to in Oslo," he said in a reference to the Palestinian interim self-rule accord launched in 1993 in the Norwegian capital.
Asked about Hebron, Netanyahu, usually fluent before the cameras, awkwardly sidestepped the question.

"I am not putting a date. I'm putting a conclusion. The satisfactory conclusion of the negotiation, I think from both sides, will be the date in which you'll be able to signify as a conclusion. And once it's concluded, I don't think there should be a delay in its implementation," he said in English.
Netanyahu sought to calm Palestinian fears that he wanted to rewrite the Oslo agreement signed by his Labour party predecessors.
"We did not propose opening the agreement. We suggested that within the confines of the existing agreement adjustments be made," he told the news conference.
Netanyahu wants to modify security arrangements for Jewish settlers in Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns to be given self-rule.
In Gaza Christopher picked up this point.
"One of the the things that has been clarified during my visit here is that the parties intend to negotiate within the four corners of the agreement," he said. "They do not seek to modify."
Asked if he was reassured by this, Arafat said: "We'll wait and see."
Arafat has sought international support for his stance. Clinton, four weeks before a presidential election, has been loathe to lean on Netanyahu, but the European Union has sought to play a role.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring arrived in Israel on Sunday and met his Israeli counterpart David Levy. Christopher seemed cool to direct European involvement, saying "any major change in the bilateral character of these negotiations is not likely to take place".
